extracted.intended_audience: literate general readers interested in social critique, club/household reform, and early-20th-century fiction/essays (including women's-club audiences)
extracted.subtask_description: Producing or evaluating social-critique essays and short fiction/lectures that combine satire, lecturing, and practical proposals (e.g., on journalism, domestic service, child-rearing). Emphasis on clarity, persuasive evidence, and social/political prescription aimed at reform-minded audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspaper content classification (truth-color scheme)
rubrics_metrics.description: A visible, categorical labeling of every part of a newspaper by truthfulness/motive: e.g., 'All intentional lies... Scarlet', 'All malicious matter... Crimson', 'All careless or ignorant mistakes... Pink', 'All for direct self-interest of owner... Dark green', 'All mere bait--to sell the paper... Bright green', 'All advertising... Brown', 'All sensational and salacious matter... Yellow', 'All hired hypocrisy... Purple', 'Good fun, instruction and entertainment... Blue', 'True and necessary news and honest editorials... Ordinary print.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a transparency device: the narrator prints papers with this color code to expose types of content. Example/observation: such labeling initially becomes a curiosity and increases sales briefly, but sustained transparency changes reader behavior and causes business models to fail; the proportion of 'blue' (good) and ordinary print grows as readers react. Anti-pattern: superficial color-coding that appears only on the face of the paper (i.e., deceptive presentation) will fool purchasers but not informed readers; long-term market effects follow from revealing truthfulness rather than mere sensational packaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalistic categories and moral distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between mere entertainment and necessary honest reporting: 'Good fun, instruction and entertainment' versus 'True and necessary news and honest editorials' and identify content motivated by owner self-interest, advertising, or sensationalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a criterion for evaluating journalism, prioritize 'true and necessary news' and honest editorials over material driven by self-interest, bait, or hired hypocrisy. The text implies that a press more faithful to truth will change public behavior and business consequences follow; editors and publishers are cautioned that labeling and honesty alter markets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological distinction: Believing versus Knowing
rubrics_metrics.description: Believing and knowing are different mental states: 'When you know a thing you don't have to believe it' — knowing is effortless and uncreditable, while believing is effortful and valorized. Rough rule: the less we know the more we believe, and vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characteristics and practical consequences: belief is fragile and resisted when challenged because it was inculcated socially (early education, ritual, threat of ostracism), while knowledge is readily revised when presented with facts. Use this distinction when constructing persuasive argument or character psychology: factual evidence will change 'knowledge' more easily, while 'belief' requires addressing emotional, social, and identity-based investment. Anti-pattern: treating belief-challenging topics as purely factual disputes without addressing the social/ritual forces that sustain belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure of human beauty and health (criterion for aesthetic/human standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Human beauty should be measured primarily by full health and vigor, right proportion, and full possession of natural powers; the human animal is by nature swift, agile, and active and should remain so throughout life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating bodies, children, or standards of beauty, prioritize physiological function, proportion related to overall body size (not isolated features), and natural activity/fitness over fashionable or arbitrary aesthetic modifications. Example: do not call a small foot 'beautiful' on an oversized body; value whole-body harmony. Anti-pattern: measuring beauty by mere ornament, costume, or isolated parts without regard to health or function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humanicultural education (curriculum standards for raising children/human improvement)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposed 'Humaniculture' curriculum: begin with theory illustrated by pictures and models; progress to practical work with living models in nursery and school; graduates would know true proportions, normal size and weight, and methods to feed, clothe, exercise, and train children to develop legitimate human beauty and power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a standard for programs that aim to improve people, combine theoretical instruction with practical, supervised experience. Concrete learning outcomes include: recognizing normal growth metrics (size/weight), understanding dietary and clothing needs to promote best growth, and prescribing appropriate exercise and training regimes. The goal is measurable improvement in health, proportion, and capability rather than mere appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: arbitrary alteration of human shape (corseting and cosmetic moulding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Altering the human shape arbitrarily — 'moulding it to lines that have nothing to do with the living structure and its complex functions' — is offensive, ridiculous, and injurious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject practices that prioritize fashionable silhouette over bodily function. Use the analogy: one would not put a corset on a horse. In design or costume choices in fiction or social practice, avoid glorifying harmful body-modifying customs; emphasize natural activity and functional form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improve people by nurture, not only by breeding (practical alternative to eugenics)
rubrics_metrics.description: While selective breeding (eugenics) could improve the species over millennia and at severe human cost, a superior method exists: improving the species after birth through conscious education and environmental measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy and cultural criterion: prioritize education, childrearing practices, and social reforms that lift average health and capability rather than relying solely on selection. Recognize obstacles in mate choice and the unpredictability of hereditary outcomes. Anti-pattern: advocating ruthless selection or neglecting social/nurtural interventions because they are slower or require public investment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domestic economy efficiency standards (centralized skilled services)
rubrics_metrics.description: Household labor is currently wasteful: many separate kitchens, stoves, and cooks produce inefficiency in labor and money. Instead, centralize services (common water, milk, baker, common cooking/cleaning establishments) run by skilled workers who live in their own homes and are respected professionals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use economies of scale and professional specialization to reduce waste and cost: example calculation given — for twenty families, three expert cooks (one at $20/week and two at $15/week) could save $150/week versus twenty individual cooks paid about $10/week each. Central purchasing reduces individual overpay and raises quality. Anti-pattern: naive 'co-operative housekeeping' that simply lumps inefficient households together without professionalization or appropriate organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employment standards for domestic servants (humane, skilled profession)
rubrics_metrics.description: Domestic service should be elevated to a respectable, well-paid profession; current expectations (e.g., enforced celibacy, cramped lodging, poor food) are exploitative and produce a high percentage of unfortunate outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a criterion for labor policy and for portrayals in writing, demand that domestic employees be allowed private homes/families, respectable wages, adequate lodging, and freedom to marry; recognize housework's skill and moral responsibilities. Depicting or designing reforms should emphasize professional dignity and social protections. Anti-pattern: treating servitude as a residual 'apprentice' role with primitive barter and loss of autonomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary meeting procedure and decorum
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard order for a club meeting: call to order, reading of minutes, officers' and committees' reports, then 'new business'; chair's use of a gavel; speakers rise when recognized; formal introductions and solemn, measured delivery for official statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In depicting or running meetings, adhere to accepted parliamentary form and ritual: correct order of business, respectful use of the gavel, formal addresses to 'Members and guests', and the ceremonial roles of officers. The text notes women being 'letter-perfect' in parliamentary usage due to repeated practice; effective chairing includes tact and measured delivery. Anti-pattern: chaotic interruptions or ignoring the standard sequence of business.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective public address in reform contexts (clarity, brevity, prepared text)
rubrics_metrics.description: An effective reform lecture/paper is 'clear, short, and to some minds convincing.' Use calm, typewritten preparation, concrete facts, economic figures, and a composed delivery to make controversial arguments persuasively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical tips for persuasive public speech: prepare a concise written text (typewritten), present clear definitions and concrete examples (e.g., economic calculations), anticipate audience disapproval, and maintain calm composure. The rhetorical effect is illustrated by Diantha: despite disapproval, the clarity and concreteness of her argument wins wholehearted support from some segments (the servant gallery). Anti-pattern: long-winded, vague or purely ideological addresses that fail to present concrete savings or practical proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of satire and demonstrative action to expose social/press failings
rubrics_metrics.description: Satirical experiments (e.g., printing truth labels on newspapers; applying truth-transparency in shops) can reveal societal hypocrisies and force readers/consumers to confront facts, but may provoke short-term popularity followed by market corrections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a creative device or reform tactic: use concrete, visible demonstrations (color-coding, public staging) to reveal inconsistencies and to alter behavior. Expect varied outcomes: temporary excitement, long-term reduction of demand for deceptive practices, and resistance from established interests. Use such devices in fiction or essay to dramatize the moral consequences of transparency versus sensationalism.
